title: Minimum wage increase on restaurant employment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
The appropriate causal method for this analysis is the Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach. This method allows us to evaluate the causal impact of the minimum wage increase on employment by comparing changes in employment for treated restaurants (those in states with the minimum wage increase) to those in control states (neighboring states without the increase), before and after the intervention. The key assumption is the parallel trends assumption, which posits that in the absence of treatment, the changes in employment trends would have been the same for both treated and control states.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# Read the dataset
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s02_data.csv")

# Simple Difference-in-Differences regression
model <- lm(y ~ treated * post, data = data)

# Coefficients
summary(model)$coefficients

# Extract the treatment effect (coefficient of treat_x_post)
treatment_effect <- coef(model)["treated:post"]

# Print the treatment effect
cat("Treatment Effect (Difference-in-Differences Estimate):", treatment_effect, "\n")

# Conduct a robustness check using clustered standard errors by group
robust_se <- coeftest(model, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~unit_id)

# Print robust standard errors
print(robust_se)

# Adding robustness check for parallel trends assumption
pre_trends_data <- data %>% filter(period < 4)
pre_trends_model <- lm(y ~ treated * factor(period), data = pre_trends_data)
summary(pre_trends_model)

# Print conclusion about pre-treatment trends
cat("Check pre-treatment trends. Coefficients for interaction terms should not be statistically significant.\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect the sign of the treatment effect (coefficient of `treated:post`) to be negative, indicating a potential reduction in employment at fast-food restaurants due to the increase in the minimum wage. The magnitude of this effect will depend on the elasticity of demand for labor in this sector, but it could be a small to moderate decrease given that fast-food employment often features low-wage jobs close to the minimum wage, making it sensitive to such policy changes. An approximate magnitude might be around -0.05 to -0.10 in log terms, suggesting a 5% to 10% reduction in the number of full-time-equivalent employees.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=high-wage states, control=neighboring states; shock=minimum wage hike
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Modest employment decline in treated restaurants post minimum wage increase
